activity: to coach a younger team by planning drills that fix a specific weakness in their passing
story:
Grayson laid the cones out in the grass before anyone arrived, ten meters apart, the same distance his brother's team kept losing the ball. He had spent two evenings thinking about it and one evening writing on graph paper, and what he had decided was this: no scrimmage today. The boys would stand between the cones and pass, and every time a pass went astray, they would do it again, immediately, with the same foot, until the ball went where it was meant to go.

The first three to arrive noticed the cones and groaned. Danny Feeney, who was eleven and had the loudest opinions, dropped his bag on the picnic table and said, "We're not scrimmaging? Coach, we always scrimmage."

"That's the problem," Grayson said. "You scrimmage every practice and you still can't complete three passes in a row. I watched the whole game Saturday. You lost the ball forty-two times."

"That's a facetious number," Danny said, though he clearly didn't know what the word meant, and neither did Grayson until he looked it up that night. Right now he only said, "It's an exact number. I counted."

They started the drill anyway. Grayson stood at the line between the cones and watched each pass, and after each one he called out what he saw: inside of the foot, hips open, look first. When Marcus bent the pass wide of the cone, Grayson made him take it again before anyone moved on. Again, and again. Marcus got frustrated, kicked the grass, then completed five in a row, and Grayson made a small check on his clipboard and did not say anything triumphant about it, because he remembered being fourteen and how praise from a coach could feel like being managed.

The harder part was the feedback. He had read about a study once, in a book his mother left on the counter, about violinists in Berlin. He'd taken a photo of the page because something about it had enthralled him, though he couldn't have said why at the time. Now, standing in his own backyard with eleven boys and a bag of nearly deflated balls, he found the photo on his phone and read the line under his breath. Ericsson, 1993. What separated the best violinists wasn't hours logged; it was effortful work on specific weaknesses, with immediate feedback. Somebody had given it a name.

"It's called deliberate practice," he told Danny, holding the phone out. "Not just doing the thing a lot. Doing the weak part, and knowing right away what went wrong."

"That's why you're making us do the boring cone thing," Danny said.

"That's why."

Danny took the phone and read the paragraph twice, his lips moving. He was the kind of kid who read everything twice, who kept a Spanish vocabulary list folded in his sock because his mother quizzed him in the car, who had once explained to the whole bench the phonetics of rolling a double r, demonstrating until the kid beside him could do it too. He handed the phone back slowly.

"Okay," he said. "But it can't only be cones. That's not a game. In a game somebody's running at you."

Grayson stopped. He looked at the cones, at the clipboard, at the graph paper in his pocket, and he understood that the kid had found the edge of what he'd planned. The study was about violinists alone in a room, and a field with opponents was a different instrument. He didn't know yet how to keep the feedback and add the pressure. "Then we do both," he said. "Cones first, then I put a defender in the passing lane, and we run the same pass until it works with someone in the way. And if that's still not like a game, we'll figure out the next thing on Thursday."

They ran it. The defender was Danny, who took the role seriously, waving his arms, calling out the passer's name the way opponents at a real match would, and the passes started arriving at the cones on the first try. Marcus, who had sulked through the first half hour, began calling for the ball in space he hadn't noticed before. When Ben tripped over a sprinkler head and sat down hard in the clover, Danny jogged over and pulled him up by both wrists before Grayson could get there, and Ben stayed in the drill.

Danny had decided, somewhere during the second round of defender drills, that this was the best practice of the season, and he wanted to know what Thursday would hold. He asked while collecting cones. He asked while pumping the flat balls back up with the hand pump Grayson's father kept in the garage. He asked a third time on the picnic table, eating the orange slices Grayson's mother had left out without being asked, and Grayson finally said, "I don't know yet. I'll figure out what's still broken and build the next thing around that."

"Okay," Danny said. He folded his Spanish list back into his sock and slung his bag over one shoulder. At the gate he turned around. "Forty-two, though. You really counted?"

activity: to compare two apartment leases and work out the total monthly cost including utilities
story:
The driving school on Route 9 smelled of burnt coffee and vinyl, and Charlie spent every waiting-room minute with two apartment leases spread across her knees. Her instructor, a patient man named Del, had learned not to comment. Between her turns behind the wheel he drank his coffee and read the paper while she worked, because her mother had been clear: Charlie could have the apartment near campus only if she proved she could figure out what it would actually cost, and the driving lesson was already paid for, so the math would happen in the gaps.

"Parallel park, then we switch," Del said from the passenger seat, and Charlie eased the car toward the curb while Lease A slid off the dashboard into the footwell. Lease A said utilities included, which she had repeated to her mother like a slogan until her mother said, slow and suspicious, "Read what 'included' includes."

She read it now, in the parking lot, while Del filled out a form on his clipboard. Water included. Trash included. Heat included. Then, in a clause so quiescent it might have hoped never to be read, a line saying that electricity was the tenant's responsibility, billed separately by the provider. Electricity. The thing that ran the lamp, the fridge, the laptop, the fan in August. She had told her mother the total was rent plus nothing, and the total was rent plus something, and the something was the something she had not checked.

"Rough day?" Del asked, glancing over. He was not the kind of instructor students lionized, the sort with stories about high-speed chases; he was quiet and thorough, and Charlie had come to prefer that.

"I found a trap in a lease," she said. "The first one says utilities included, but that only means the utilities it lists. Electricity isn't on the list." She held the page out, and he looked at it without taking it from her, tapping the clause with one finger.

"Fine print," he said. "That's where they hide things."

The second lease, Lease B, from the building her cousin Rosa was already raving about, said nothing sweeping at all. Instead it assigned each utility its own line: tenant pays electric, tenant pays internet, landlord covers water and heat. Lower rent, too. Charlie copied the numbers into her notebook, column by column, and discovered that if electricity in the city averaged what the provider's website said it averaged, Lease A and Lease B landed within twenty dollars of each other, close enough that the cheaper-looking one was not cheaper, only honest in a different way.

That was the afternoon she thought about her father, three years ago, signing the papers for the shop he'd wanted for a decade. He had lionized the landlord at the closing, called him the last fair man in the county, and six months later stood in the empty storefront reading a clause about "standard maintenance" that turned out to mean only the pipes, not the wiring, not the roof. Charlie had been thirteen, sitting on a folding chair with a juice box, watching his face change. He hadn't blamed anyone out loud. He'd just said, "Words mean what they say, not what I want them to mean," and she had carried that sentence around since, not fully understanding it until now, in a driving school parking lot, with two leases and a Tuesday evening going dim around her.

A boy about her age, waiting for his lesson, leaned over from the next chair. He had been circling listings on his phone for half an hour. "That first one's got utilities included, right? That's the one I'd take."

"Check the list," Charlie said. She turned the page so he could see. "Included only covers what's actually named. Electricity's missing." He read the clause, went pale in the fluorescent light, and started scrolling back through his own listing with his thumb moving fast. She slid her notebook over so he could see her two columns, the rent plus the electric line, the totals almost twins.

"That's it, then," he said. "The other one's better."

"I don't know yet," Charlie said. "They're about even, and I haven't called about internet. So I'm not done deciding." She said it plainly, and it felt like the first honest sentence she'd built all day.

Del rapped the roof of the car. "Your turn behind the wheel, Charlie. Bring the paperwork."

She gathered the leases, folded them along the same creases, and slid them into the folder under the notebook, then pulled the door shut and checked her mirror.

activity: to analyse an unreliable narrator in a novel and how the point of view shapes the reader's trust
story:
The bus smelled of diesel and the sweet decay of someone's forgotten banana, and Alyssa had fifteen minutes to figure out what she actually believed about Holden Caulfield before the bell rang for her English seminar. The essay prompt sat folded on her knee: whether a narrator who admits to lying can still be trusted, and what that admission does to the reader. She had read the book twice, once at fourteen and again last weekend, and the second time had felt like meeting a boy she already knew and noticing, for the first time, that he never stopped talking.

Marcus slid into the seat across the aisle, holding his copy with one finger jammed in the spine like a bookmark. "Okay," he said, "so he tells us right at the start. Page whatever. 'I'm the most terrific liar you ever saw in your life.' His exact words. And then he keeps going for two hundred pages like we're just supposed to take his word for everything." Marcus liked to arrive at problems the way other people arrived at parties, loudly and expecting company.

"So don't take his word," Alyssa said. She was testing something out, the way you test a handrail before committing your weight. "That's the whole point, isn't it? The book came out in 1951, and everybody since has had to decide how much of Holden's story to believe after he admits he lies. Maybe the admission is the trick."

Marcus frowned at the seatback in front of him, which was upholstered in a friable kind of vinyl that crumbled like dry cheese wherever students picked at it, and everyone picked at it. "The trick how? He's just being honest about being dishonest. That's like a magician announcing the cards are fake."

"Except a magician announces it and then you watch anyway." She pulled her notebook out and wrote liar in the margin, then circled it, then drew the circle so many times it became a small black sun. "You watch harder. You start catching things. He says he's tapping Ackley on the shoulder to say goodnight, and then he admits the whole thing was a lie, and you realize you'd been picturing it, feeling almost sorry for him, and he was making it up the whole time." She tapped her pen against the notebook. "Every lie he confesses circumscribes him, in a way. It draws a line around what he can't face saying straight."

"That's very fancy," Marcus said. "My man just needs a nap and a therapist."

"That's also true," Alyssa said, and surprised herself by laughing. "Both things can be true. That might be the answer. He's a mess and he's doing something deliberate on purpose, and the book won't tell you which one is running the show because it can't. He's the one talking."

The bus hit the pothole by the church on Delancey, and every book in the back rows jumped an inch. Their teacher, Mr. Reyes, was riding up front, headphones on, oblivious, and Alyssa felt a brief flare of resentment that he got to sit in silence while she had to solve this with Marcus before first period. But then she thought about the word "phony," Holden's favorite weapon, and she thought about etymology, which she'd looked up on Sunday because she couldn't help herself: how a word's history can hide a second meaning inside it, the way "sincere" was supposed to come from without wax, a statue with nothing filling its cracks. Holden called everyone phony. Holden lied about everything. The words were a confession wearing a costume.

"So what's your thesis?" Marcus asked. "Because I'm writing 'you can't trust him and you can't stop listening,' and calling it a night."

"That's actually not bad," she admitted. The admission cost her something; she'd been planning to say it first.

The bus swung into the school loop, brakes sighing, and Mr. Reyes took his headphones off and stood in the aisle like a man surfacing from deep water. That was when the twist arrived, and it arrived the way real ones do, through Marcus's mouth, casually, as he stood up. "Also, forgot to tell you. The essay's due Thursday, not today. Reyes moved it. Check the portal." Alyssa stared at him, and then at her notebook, at the small black sun she'd spent the whole ride drawing around a word, and she felt the specific vertigo of having worked very hard at the wrong time for reasons she couldn't regret. She closed the notebook anyway, keeping her thumb in it, and followed Marcus down the steps into the cold.

"So Thursday," Marcus said on the sidewalk, bouncing on his heels. "Does that mean you'll have it figured out?"

"Nobody has it figured out," Alyssa said. "That's the point of the book." She hugged the notebook to her chest and started toward the doors. "Ask me again in 1951."

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
story:
The choir room at St. Brigid's smelled of dust and old hymnals, and Natalie had claimed the corner table by the window because it was the only one where the afternoon light fell across manuscript paper without glare. Mr. Ruiz, the organist, had agreed to teach her composition on Thursday afternoons in exchange for her singing alto on Sundays, an arrangement her mother called an answer to prayer and her brother called suspiciously cheap labor. Four weeks in, Natalie had learned to notate a melody in the treble clef, to keep her bars even, and to distrust the way her own hand smoothed every phrase into something safe.

The assignment was sixteen bars with chord changes, and the problem was the sixteenth bar. Or rather, every bar. She had written a melody she liked in her head, something that rose the way the alleluia rose at the Easter vigil, but when she counted it out on paper, each of her closing phrases came up short. She tapped her pencil against the window and counted again, mouthing one-two-three-four, and the phrase that had felt so full in the air felt thin on the staff, a beat missing, the last note landing early and leaving an emptiness after it.

"You look like someone stole your lunch," said Desiree, who had come in to fetch her jacket from the piano bench. Desiree was nineteen, home from her first year of college, and she had a way of standing in doorways as though she hadn't decided yet whether to stay.

"My bar's wrong," Natalie said. "It's supposed to have four beats and it only has three, and I can't just stuff another note in there because then it sounds like a machine."

Desiree came over and looked at the page. She hummed the phrase, tapping four fingers on the table, and then she pointed at the half note Natalie had written to end the bar. "That's two beats," she said. "You wrote it right, your count's right, the phrase just wants more than you gave it." She slid the pencil back across the table to Natalie and did not say anything else, which was either kindness or laziness, and Natalie couldn't decide which.

Natalie stared at the half note. Half was two beats. She needed three. She thought about the way a bell at the vigil seemed to keep sounding after it had finished sounding, about the way her grandmother held the last word of a hymn as if letting it down gently from a height. She drew a small dot after the half note, then counted: the note, and the dot, one-two-three, and the fourth beat of silence before the next bar began, and the bar was full. The dot after a note added half the note's value, she realized, which meant her dotted half note now lasted exactly three beats in four-four time, and the emptiness she'd heard was the fourth beat arriving like a held breath, not a hole.

She wrote the sixteenth bar that way and played it through on the piano in the sanctuary while Mr. Ruiz vacuumed the aisle carpet, a sound like distant weather. The dotted note hung there and resolved, and something in her chest loosened. She had been thinking of rhythm as a fence, she decided, as something that circumscribed the melody, when actually the rhythm was the ground the melody stood on, and a held note was not a delay but a kind of attention.

That night her grandmother sent her a message on the phone Natalie had given her for her birthday, typed slowly and formally, like a letter that had learned to travel through wires. Natalie, your mother says you are writing music at the church now. When I was sixteen my father told me that music was for worship and not for girls who wanted to show off, and I stopped. I want you to know that I have thought about that for sixty years and I still do not know if he was right. He was a serious man and not a charlatan, whatever else he was. I would like to hear what you write, even the parts that show off. Especially those. Grandmother.

Natalie read it three times. She knew the story in outline, the piano lessons abandoned, the church her great-grandfather had helped build, but she had never heard her grandmother admit to not knowing whether a choice had been right. In Natalie's family, choices were either righteous or regrettable, and the categories were assigned early and permanently. Her grandmother's uncertainty felt seismic, a small plate shifting under a floor she'd assumed was solid. It also felt like permission, though permission to what, exactly, she couldn't have said.

The next Thursday she brought the manuscript to choir practice and set it on the piano. Desiree was there, and Mr. Ruiz, and two of the sopranos who were always early. "Play it," Desiree said, and Natalie did, all sixteen bars, her fingers clumsy on the chord changes, the dotted phrases landing where they were supposed to land. When she finished, one of the sopranos said it was pretty, in the tone people used for children's drawings, and Mr. Ruiz said the harmony in bar nine didn't agree with itself yet, and Desiree said nothing, only tapped the sixteenth bar with her finger twice, the way you'd touch a bruise you were proud of.

Afterward, in the parking lot, Natalie sat in her mother's car and looked at the manuscript on her lap. She was starting to hear two arguments in her head at once: her great-grandfather's, that music belonged to the church and should serve it humbly, and her own, newer one, that a dotted half note was already an argument, that holding a sound for three beats when two would do was a small act of wanting more, and that wanting more could be a form of reverence instead of vanity. She could not get the two positions to merge cleanly. Maybe they weren't supposed to. Maybe her grandmother's sixty years of not knowing had been the honest version all along.

She texted a photo of the sixteenth bar to her grandmother, the dotted note visible, and typed, "Can I play it for you Sunday after the service?" Then she sat with the phone in her hand, watching the screen, the parking lot lights coming on one by one along the fence.

Three dots appeared at the bottom of the screen, and vanished, and appeared again.
